questions.q: What problem do time-slicing and MIG both exist to solve?
options: That large training jobs cannot use more than one GPU at a time
That GPU quota requests take too long to approve
That Terraform cannot provision more than one GPU VM per region
That a pod given a whole GPU under the default model often leaves most of that GPU's capacity idle
questions.explain: Since nvidia.com/gpu is allocated as a whole unit by default, a workload needing only a fraction of a GPU's capacity still claims the entire thing, leaving the rest idle. Time-slicing and MIG are two different answers to that waste.

questions.q: What does GPU time-slicing actually provide, and what does it NOT provide?
options: It provides hardware-level memory isolation between sharing pods
It only works on GPUs with MIG support
It provides software-based sharing of one physical GPU across multiple pods, but no memory or fault isolation between them
It permanently partitions the GPU into separate physical devices
questions.explain: Time-slicing lets the device plugin advertise multiple replicas of nvidia.com/gpu mapped to the same physical card, with the GPU's scheduler context-switching between them — but all sharing pods still share the full memory pool with no isolation.

questions.q: What makes Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) fundamentally different from time-slicing?
options: MIG is a pure software scheduling feature with no hardware involvement
MIG partitions the GPU at the hardware level into isolated instances with dedicated memory and compute, available only on supporting GPUs like the A100 and H100
MIG is only usable outside of Kubernetes
MIG allows unlimited partitions on any NVIDIA GPU
questions.explain: MIG is a hardware capability of specific GPUs (A100, H100-class) that creates genuinely isolated GPU instances with their own memory and compute slices — real isolation, not just scheduling fairness, and limited to supporting hardware.

questions.q: In a MIG profile name like 1g.10gb, what do the two parts of the name represent?
options: The compute-slice fraction and the memory allotted to that instance
The GPU generation and the driver version
The number of pods allowed and the node's total memory
The time-slicing replica count and the CUDA version
questions.explain: The number before "g" is the fraction of compute slices assigned to that GPU instance, and the number after is the amount of dedicated memory — e.g. 1g.10gb is one compute slice with 10 GB of memory.

questions.q: Which workload is the best fit for GPU sharing (time-slicing or MIG) rather than a dedicated whole GPU?
options: A single large model-training job that needs maximum throughput from one GPU
A distributed training run spanning multiple GPU VMs
A checkpoint-and-resume training job recovering from a failure
Several small, low/medium-traffic inference services that each use only a fraction of a GPU's capacity
questions.explain: Sharing mechanisms exist to avoid wasting idle GPU capacity on light workloads. Large training jobs still want a whole GPU, or several, dedicated to themselves — sharing is squarely an inference and multi-tenant problem.
